messages.author: 3a775dfa0a96bf95
messages.subject: Reporting on repeated rows
parts:
---plyr 1.5.2 on R 2.13.0, Windows 7 64-bit---

I have a dataset with (intentionally) repeated rows and I want to report on the number of repetitions.

The following code works:

row.counts <- function (r)
    arrange(
       ddply(r,
             names(r),   # all columns
             function(a) cbind(a[1,],count=nrow(a))),
       desc(count))

> test <- data.frame(a=c(1,2,3,1,2,3),b=c(1,2,1,2,2,1))
> row.counts(test)
  a b count
1 2 2     2
2 3 1     2
3 1 1     1
4 1 2     1

... but doesn't seem very elegant.

Next, I wanted the rows within each group with the same count to be ordered lexicographically.  The best I could come up with was

row.counts.sort <- function (r) {
    counted <-
       ddply(r,
             names(r),
             function(a) cbind(a[1,],count=nrow(a)))
    arrange(counted,desc(count),do.call(order,counted))
}

Can someone do better?  ... or suggest extensions/changes to plyr which would handle these cases more elegantly? 

             -s

Yup, that's it!  Thanks for the quick and helpful reply!

But wouldn't it be more consistent with the plyr paradigm to have it called like this (a la subset and mutate)?:

ddply( test, ...columns..., count )

The main problem there is specifying all columns.  Count lets you do that by omitting the column spec:

count(test, ) == count(test, vars=NULL)

but ddply (reasonably enough) does not:

> ddply(test,,function(r) cbind(r[1,],freq=nrow(r)))
Error in as.quoted(.variables) :                                          <<<< no default
  argument ".variables" is missing, with no default

And an explicit NULL variable spec means the opposite of what it does in count.  The ddply definition seems more consistent: .() = NULL means no grouping variables.  Perhaps TRUE can mean all grouping variables, something like Top.

> ddply(test,.variables=NULL,function(r) cbind(r[1,],freq=nrow(r)))
   .id a b freq                                                                    <<<< NULL means NO variables, not ALL variables
1 <NA> 1 1    6

The signatures are inconsistent, too:

> args(ddply)

function (.data, .variables, .fun = NULL, ..., .progress = "none", .drop = TRUE, .parallel = FALSE) 

> args(count)

function (df, vars = NULL, wt_var = NULL) 

Why df vs. .data and vars vs. .variables?  .progress doesn't seem necessary for count, but .drop certainly makes sense.

           -s
